news_drafts.headline: Castle Point forecasts £4.5m General Fund overspend for 2026/27 after £2.1m gap in 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
Castle Point Council is forecasting a £4.5m overspend on its day-to-day General Fund budget for 2026/27, Cabinet was told on 14 October, with probable outcomes between £4m and £5m. The figure rests on one quarter's data and a line-by-line budget review is continuing. The main pressures are £1.3m on salaries, £0.8m of income that will not be achieved, £0.9m of legal costs for planning appeals and the Castle Point Plan, and £0.55m on temporary accommodation.

The 2025/26 outturn (the actual figures once the year had ended) showed a General Fund overspend of £2.126m before use of reserves. Drawing on money set aside for housing and another earmarked fund cut it to £0.431m, which the council's general reserve absorbs. That reserve falls to £4.471m, which is £1.371m above its approved minimum of £3.1m. Housing carried the largest pressure: £1.225m on temporary accommodation and £340k on mainly interim staff. In the separate housing revenue account, funded by rents, the overspend was £0.891m, with £526k from staffing. For 2026/27 that account is forecast to overspend by £674k, to come from its unallocated reserves, which would fall to almost zero.

The papers say the 2025/26 overspend was not forecast in quarterly reports to Cabinet on 16 September 2025, 23 December 2025 or 18 March 2026. An investigation is under way, and the council is talking to its external auditors about the 2025/26 audit. The interim chief finance officer's review found structural issues in the budget that imply a similar trajectory for 2026/27 and later years unless corrective action is taken. The papers say £400k of waste and recycling overspend on tipping and recycling costs was "reasonably predictable".

news_drafts.headline: Castle Point admits unquantified financial risk in housing enforcement policy
news_drafts.lead: Castle Point Council has adopted a housing enforcement policy that allows it to carry out remedial works on properties where landlords have breached safety standards, then recharged the costs to the responsible party. However, the council's own papers acknowledge "an unknown unquantified risk from the individuals not being able to pay," creating potential bad debts that could fall back on the council. The policy was approved without an estimate of this exposure, and the council asserts the policy requires no new budget provision, despite the admitted liability risk. The three-year policy covers 2026 to 2029.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Council achieved regulatory upgrade from C4 to C3 for social housing services but movement toward C2 and modern IT system implementation are creating near-term budget pressure.
findings.detail: The Council has moved from C4 to C3 consumer standards Regulatory Judgement for social housing services, described as 'a significant achievement'. The Council is working toward C2 designation and implementing a modern housing IT system with integration and automation intended to generate future savings. However, these measures have increased pressure on both the General Fund and HRA budgets in the short term.
findings.matters: Regulatory upgrade demonstrates service improvement and compliance delivery but near-term cost increases create upward budget pressure requiring efficiency gains; the IT investment carries typical implementation cost/benefit timing risks.
findings.quote: The Council has recently succeeded in moving from a C4 to a C3 consumer standards Regulatory Judgement for its social housing services. This is a significant achievement, but it has not been inexpensive. The Council is now working towards a C2 designation, including the implementation of a modern housing IT system with the integration and automation needed to generate future savings.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: LGA Corporate Peer Challenge noted limited progress on finance approach and identified need for more robust approaches to forecasting and managing financial position.
findings.detail: The LGA Corporate Peer Challenge follow-up report in November 2025 noted progress on operational improvements but identified scepticism from officers and elected members regarding robustness and effectiveness of finance and budget-setting processes. The report stated that finance is an area where progress against recommendations has been limited.
findings.matters: External peer challenge assessment of weak finance governance, combined with demonstrated forecasting failures and structural budget issues, creates a composite picture of financial management weakness material to lender assessment of council creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The approach to finance is an area in which progress against the corporate peer challenge recommendations would appear to be limited. We see a need to develop more robust, collective and transparent approaches to forecasting and managing the authority's financial position.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Budget identified as hard to interrogate due to convoluted internal recharges obscuring base position; Cabinet approved budget re-basing to increase transparency.
findings.detail: The interim finance director identified that the budget has proven hard to interrogate with convoluted internal recharges obscuring the base position. This makes it more challenging for budget holders to be held accountable or manage their budgets effectively. Cabinet approved re-basing of budgets, simplifying internal recharges to statutory required levels, and adjusting service budgets for technical accounting adjustments. New centralised processes for legal, IT and property spending are being implemented.
findings.matters: Budget opacity and inability of budget holders to control their own variances signals financial management infrastructure failure; while re-basing is welcome, the prior lack of identification is concerning to lenders.
findings.figures: £8,335k base budget approved for re-basing and simplification
findings.quote: Overall, the budget has proven hard to interrogate with convoluted internal recharges obscuring the base position. This also makes it more challenging for budget holders to be held to account or for them to manage their budgets effectively. To ensure transparency and to ensure the budget is soundly set, the budget will need correcting.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation pause has invalidated prior planning assumptions and required Council to address reserves spent in anticipation of vesting day obligations.
findings.detail: The pausing of LGR has created significant uncertainty. The Council had made decisions assuming LGR on 1 April 2028, spending reserves at higher levels to fund improvements necessary to meet Vesting Day obligations. With LGR now delayed, the Council must work with neighbouring councils to recover resources from Central Government if possible and refocus resources assuming LGR will be delayed or may not happen. The LGR budget line shows £250k allocation for 2026/27, now presumed to be repurposed.
findings.matters: The LGR pause invalidates a strategic planning assumption; reserves spent in anticipation of merger economies of scale must now be replaced through other means, adding to structural deficit pressure.
findings.figures: LGR budget £250k (2026/27) showing £236k favourable variance as budget presumed to be re-purposed
findings.quote: LGR pausing has created significant uncertainty through local government and, at the time of writing this report, there was no guidance or further information from Government as to the scope or duration of the pause, or its likely outcomes. [...] Now LGR is delayed, it will need to work with neighbouring councils to recover resources from Central Government if possible and to refocus and rebuild its own resources on the assumption that LGR, will be delayed, if it happens at all.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 Report: Medium Term Financial Strategy - Cabinet - 14/10/2026
findings.headline: Without corrective action, Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support by 2028/29 to balance budget.
findings.detail: Finance modelling shows that if no action is taken, the Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support by 2028/29. The modelling demonstrates a trajectory where a recurring overspend of approximately £4.5 million continues annually. The Section 151 Officer has indicated members will not tolerate an imbalanced budgetary position and that the MTFP must be sustainable and credibly deliverable.
findings.matters: A trajectory toward requiring Extraordinary Financial Support signals the council has moved from transient pressures to structural imbalance and represents formal escalation of financial distress with external intervention risk.
findings.figures: £4.467 million recurring deficit 2026/27 onwards; cumulative savings requirement £8.5 million by 2031/32; opening reserves £23.017 million declining to nil by 2028/29 in no-action scenario
findings.quote: Finance has modelled the position to demonstrate what would happen if no action was taken. Very clearly, it evidences that by 2028/29, the Council would require Extraordinary Financial Support (EFS) to balance its budget.
